planting.note: Plant bulbs six weeks before the ground freezes so roots establish ahead of winter dormancy.

directions: This heirloom Dutch hyacinth carries soft apricot-salmon blooms that shift toward pale peach as flowers age, a warm departure from the blues and pinks common in the group. Set bulbs in well-drained soil enriched with compost, pointed side up, at a depth of about six inches. Water thoroughly after planting and again in early spring as shoots emerge, then let foliage die back naturally to recharge the bulb for next year. In warmer zones chill bulbs in a refrigerator for six to eight weeks before planting to ensure reliable flowering.

planting.note: Plant bulbs in autumn once soil has cooled but well before hard frost locks the ground.

directions: Aiolos produces dense, pure white flower spikes with a strong, sweet fragrance that makes it a favorite for forcing indoors as well as garden borders. Space bulbs a few inches apart in loose, fertile, well-draining soil and plant them roughly three times as deep as the bulb is tall. Keep soil evenly moist through the bloom period but avoid waterlogging, which encourages bulb rot. For forced winter bloom, chill bulbs in the dark near 40 degrees Fahrenheit for ten to twelve weeks before bringing them into warmth and light.

planting.note: Plant small bulbs in early to mid fall so they naturalize before the first hard freeze.

directions: This pure white sport of Siberian squill brightens early spring lawns and woodland edges before tree canopies fill in, and it self-seeds readily to form drifts over the years. Plant the small bulbs about three inches deep in humus-rich soil that stays moist in spring but can dry out somewhat once the foliage yellows in early summer. It tolerates being naturalized directly into turf, since its foliage matures and fades before regular mowing resumes. Leave seed capsules intact if you want colonies to spread naturally, or deadhead promptly if you prefer to keep the pure white form from reverting toward blue seedlings nearby.
